The Priesthood of the Ancestors

The priests of the Ancestor Gods tend the temples in the Deep of Renown of every hold: Hearth Priests of Valaya who heal and keep the hearth, Forge Priests of Grungni and Smednir who guard the works of the ancestors, and Doom Priests of Grimnir who keep the warrior cults and witness the Slayers' oaths. There is no single head of the faith. Each temple runs itself, its priests drawn from the old Runesmith clans, and the High Priests of Grungni and Valaya sit on their king's council.
The eldest of the High Priests. The Dawi faith has no supreme head, but the others listen when this one speaks.

Ancestral Lore
Tell the Tales of the Ancestors
Gather the hold at the long table and tell the old tales of the Ancestor Gods, as the priests have done since the Golden Age, pausing only for a respectful gulp of ale.
Take a Calling
Devote yourself to one aspect of the faith: the hearth of Valaya, the forge of Grungni and Smednir, or the war shrines of Grimnir.
Keep a Holy Day
Lead the hold in the holy day of your calling. Every day is a workday to the Dawi, save the days of the Ancestor Gods.
Speak at the King's Council
Take your place on the council, as the High Priests of Grungni and Valaya always have, and speak for the ancestors.
Bless the Throng
Walk the ranks before the march, mark the warriors' brows with the rune of their clan, and remind them of the ancestors who are watching.
Tend the Wounded
Always provide aid to a wounded or ailing Dawi, says Valaya's stricture. Heal yourself or a wounded or sick member of your court.
Inscribe a Master Rune
A High Priest may inscribe the master rune of the god of the calling. It is three years' work, and no priest does it twice.
Consecrate a Temple
Raise a great vaulted temple to the Ancestor Gods at your capital, its walls carved with their deeds and a lectern on the dais for the High Priest.

[Root.GetTitledFirstName],

The elders of the temple have spoken with your clan's priests and heard your answers to the old questions. You will take the initiate's hood and learn the tales by heart, as we learned them from those before us. Nothing of the faith is written down that can be told instead. Come to the Deep of Renown at first bell.

[From.GetFirstName], High Priest
I will come.

The long table is full and the fire is banked high. The hold has come to hear the old tales, and every face turns to you as you rise. A priest can talk for hours of the ancestors and the Dawi will listen to every word, provided the tankards stay full. Which tale shall it be tonight?
Grungni, who dug the first mine and taught us to find the gold.
Valaya, who founded the first holds and gave us the runes.
Grimnir, who went north alone to close the gates of Chaos.

There is no rivalry between the gods of the Dawi, and every priest keeps every god's holy days. Yet each priest is called, sooner or later, to one temple above the others. The elders say it is time you chose yours.
The hearth of Valaya: healing, home and honoured guests.
The forge of Grungni and Smednir: the works of the ancestors.
The war shrines of Grimnir: the warrior cults and the Slayers.

It is Mitterfruhl, Valaya's day. The doors of every home are open, the hearths are swept and lit afresh, and you walk the halls with the sheaf of barley and the ale cup, blessing each hearth and each beardling as the goddess blessed the first holds.

It is First Quaff, one of Grungni's four great days, and the first barrels of the year are tapped beneath the statue of the god with a tankard in each hand. You speak the blessing over the brewhouse and the forges while the whole hold waits, thirstily, for you to finish.

Grimnir has no festivals. His day is the eve of battle. Tonight the warriors of the hold keep vigil at his war shrine, axes laid before the altar, and you tell them of the Long Migration and the Coming of Chaos until the sky outside grows grey.

It is the Day of Remembrance, and the whole hold gathers in the Deep of Renown to hear the deeds of the ancestors read out from the Book of Remembrance. You read until your voice is hoarse, and no one leaves early.
Lead the rites.

The council sits in the old hall, longbeards on the stone benches and the king on the dais, and the priests' seat is at the king's right hand, as it has been since the Golden Age. The talk is of quarrels between the clans, of debts and old wrongs. When it falls quiet, every head turns to you.
Speak for peace among the clans.
Speak the old law, as the ancestors wrote it.

The throng is drawn up in the gate hall, rank on rank of iron and gromril. You walk the lines with the clan runes painted wet on your hands, marking each warrior's brow, and you remind them that the ancestors are watching from their halls, and will know who stood and who did not.
Let the ancestors see.

Valaya's stricture is plain: always provide aid to a wounded or ailing Dawi. You open the temple's chest of balms and salves, put the kettle on the fire, and pour the first ale. If in doubt, the first lesson of the rites of healing says, serve more ale.
Hold still. This will sting.

Three years you have worked at the anvil in the temple's forge, striking the rune of your god in the old way, one stroke a day at the hour the ancestors laid down. Today the last stroke rang true, and the rune woke and glowed in the dark of the temple.
It is done.

The masons have carved the last of the reliefs, the deeds of the gods on every wall, and the lectern stands on its dais opposite the great doors. The hold crowds the vaulted hall for its first rite, as many as fit in a king's audience hall. It will stand as long as the mountain does.
Let the doors stand open.

An old miner of the hold is dying, and he has sent for you. He wants to name what goes into his tomb with him before his heirs, as the custom is, and he wants the words of Gazul's Ritual of Passage said over him so his spirit finds the way to the Halls of the Ancestors.
Sit with him, as Gazul asks.
Send for a priest of Gazul.

A young Dawi waits at the temple door with his head already half shaved. He has shamed himself and his clan, and he will not say how. He has come to swear the Slayer's oath, and he asks a Doom Priest to witness it and cut the first tattoo of his shame into his skin.

A young Dawi waits at the temple door with his head already half shaved. He has shamed himself and his clan, and he will not say how. He has come to swear the Slayer's oath. That is for the Doom Priests of Grimnir to witness, not for you.
Kneel. I will witness it.
Send him on to the Doom Priests.

A beardling has been born in the hold, and its parents bring the child to the temple for Valaya's blessing, wrapped in the clan's colours. You hold it up before the statue of the goddess with the infant in her arm and the tankard in her hand, and say the old words over it.
Valaya keep you, little one.

A clan from a fallen hold has brought you a suit of gromril armour, dented and black with age, recovered from the ruins where their ancestor fell. It is the closest thing the Dawi have to a holy relic: the work of a master long dead. They ask that it be honoured.
Restore it, stroke by stroke.
Set it in the Deep of Renown for all to honour.
